content: Orlistat is indicated for patients with a pretreatment BMI greater than 30 kg/m² or a BMI greater than 27 kg/m² in the presence of additional risk factors or comorbidities such as hypertension (HTN), diabetes mellitus (DM), or hyperlipidemia. The prescription form (Xenical) is administered as 120 mg orally every 8 hours with each fat-containing meal, either during the meal or up to 1 hour afterward. Doses exceeding 120 mg three times daily do not provide additional benefits. The over-the-counter form (Alli) is available as up to 60 mg orally every 8 hours with each fat-containing meal. Orlistat is only effective when used as an adjunct to caloric restriction, increased physical activity, and behavioral modification. The safety and efficacy of orlistat in patients under 12 years of age have not been established. Orlistat may reduce the effects of triheptanoin by decreasing exposure to its metabolite, heptanoate. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be considered. Orlistat decreases the levels or effects of abacavir by inhibiting gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and monitoring is recommended. Loss of virological control has been reported in HIV-infected patients taking orlistat concomitantly with antiretroviral drugs. The exact mechanism is unclear but may involve drug-drug interactions that inhibit systemic absorption of the antiretroviral agent. HIV RNA levels should be monitored frequently, and if an increased viral load is confirmed, orlistat should be discontinued. Orlistat decreases the levels of acetazolamide, amiodarone, atazanavir, beta-carotene, carbamazepine, clobazam, clonazepam, clorazepate, cyclosporine, darunavir, diazepam, didanosine, dolutegravir, doxercalciferol, efavirenz, elvitegravir, emtricitabine, enfuvirtide, eslicarbazepine acetate, ethosuximide, ethotoin, etravirine, ezogabine, felbamate, fosamprenavir, fosphenytoin, gabapentin, indinavir, lamivudine, lamotrigine, lacosamide, levetiracetam, levothyroxine, lorazepam, maraviroc, methsuximide, nelfinavir, nevirapine, oxcarbazepine, paricalcitol, perampanel, phenobarbital, phenytoin, pregabalin, primidone, raltegravir, rilpivirine, ritonavir, and other drugs by inhibiting GI absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. For drugs such as cyclosporine, administration should be separated by at least 3 hours. For levothyroxine, administration should be separated by 4 hours to reduce the risk of hypothyroidism. For doxercalciferol and paricalcitol, administration should be separated by 2 hours. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required for drugs associated with a risk of seizures, such as anticonvulsants (e.g., carbamazepine, clobazam, clonazepam, ethosuximide, gabapentin, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, pregabalin, primidone, and others). In HIV-infected patients, loss of virological control has been reported with concomitant use of orlistat and antiretroviral drugs such as atazanavir, darunavir, efavirenz, elvitegravir, emtricitabine, enfuvirtide, indinavir, lamivudine, maraviroc, nelfinavir, nevirapine, raltegravir, rilpivirine, and ritonavir. The exact mechanism is unclear but may involve drug-drug interactions that inhibit systemic absorption of the antiretroviral agent. HIV RNA levels should be monitored frequently, and if an increased viral load is confirmed, orlistat should be discontinued. In summary, orlistat interacts with a wide range of medications by inhibiting their GI absorption, potentially reducing their therapeutic effects. These interactions necessitate careful monitoring, dose adjustments, and in some cases, separation of administration times to mitigate risks.
